title: Good Enough Is a Strategy

Someone across the table told me we’d regret it. I’ve thought about that meeting more than it deserves, mostly because we didn’t regret it. The thing went out. People used it. The missing feature turned out to be something we’d imagined they wanted and they hadn’t. That is the whole essay. Here is the longer version. The dish that never leaves the kitchen There is a persistent myth in tech that the best product wins. Build the most complete feature set, hit the highest quality bar, plate the most polished experience, and the market will recognise it. This belief is deeply held, widely shared, and expensive. It is also wrong often enough to deserve a challenge. Picture the meal that only exists in the kitchen. It is perfectly seasoned. The plating is immaculate. Nobody has tasted it, because the chef keeps sending it back for one more adjustment. Meanwhile your guests are eating somewhere else. That dish is what “perfect” looks like: technically excellent, and technically not dinner. “Good enough” is not a concession. In the right conditions, it is a deliberate and highly effective strategic choice. The bar was SMS, not perfection Take WhatsApp. When it launched, most product teams considered messaging a solved problem. BlackBerry Messenger had read receipts. Skype had video. AIM had a decade of loyalty. WhatsApp offered text, delivered reliably, no ads, almost no interface. That was it. Nothing about it was technically impressive. The design was borderline spartan. The feature set was aggressively limited. WhatsApp now has over two billion users. BlackBerry Messenger is defunct. So what happened? In markets where speed and reliability matter, the product that does one thing well usually beats the product that does everything adequately. WhatsApp was good enough to replace SMS. That was the bar. Not out-featuring every messaging app; just being better than the default, in the places that mattered, at the moment you reached for your phone. The team was ruthless about scope, because scope is where speed goes to die. Britannica plated beautifully Now consider Wikipedia. Encyclopaedia Britannica spent decades building the most authoritative reference work in human history. Encarta was polished, well-funded, full of multimedia and search, a far more compelling experience than a wiki assembled by volunteers. Early Wikipedia was, to put it kindly, uneven. Articles ranged from excellent to embarrassing. The editing process was chaotic and occasionally a knife fight. Wikipedia won. Completely. It now handles over 17 billion page views a month. Encarta was discontinued in 2009. Britannica survives as a shadow of itself. Britannica plated beautifully. Wikipedia just kept feeding people, and kept getting better while it did. The “good enough” content model, collaboratively produced and imperfect and instantly updatable, outcompeted curated excellence on every dimension users actually valued: speed, breadth, accessibility, freshness. Press enter or click to view image in full size Source: Pexels Constraints are a recipe, not a compromise The Kindle is the same story with a different flavour. When Amazon launched it in 2007, e-readers with fancier features already existed. The Kindle’s industrial design was deliberately plain. It didn’t play video. It browsed the web badly. Its interface was less slick than a Sony Reader. What it did was make buying and reading a book fast and frictionless, with something close to obsession. Everything that diluted the core job got cut. The Kindle won not in spite of its constraints but partly because of them. Constraints forced a decision about what the thing was for. Here is where I have to be careful with you, because “good enough” is not a licence to serve people something raw. Good enough, but not in the wrong places The companies that win this way share a disciplined, slightly cold-blooded clarity about which dimensions of quality matter to a person making a real choice. WhatsApp wasn’t good enough on features; it was exceptional on reliability and simplicity, the two axes that mattered to anyone leaving SMS. Wikipedia wasn’t good enough for a citation; it was exceptional for settling an argument at dinner. The Kindle wasn’t good enough as a media tablet; it was exceptional as a reading device. Knowing which slice of quality actually matters is the hard part. Shipping the rest at eighty percent is easy once you know that. The real failure mode isn’t shipping bad products. It’s shipping food that looks great and is cold in the middle: acceptable on surface polish, unreliable on the core. Those products don’t win. They collect one-star reviews and churn quietly for years before anyone admits it. The perfectionism cult builds elaborate reasons to keep the plate in the kitchen. There is always an edge case, an uncovered scenario, a design detail that isn’t quite right. Sometimes that’s worth fixing first. But the question is always: compared to what? The cost of perfect isn’t zero. It’s weeks of not being in market, not learning from real people, not compounding on feedback that would have told you what mattered. Speed of iteration is itself a kind of quality. The product that learns fastest tends to end up better than the one that launched best. Press enter or click to view image in full
